samples.summary: SSRF gate: the "same listener as the configured server" exemption allows a URL when ANY ONE of its resolved addresses matches the server, skipping the private-address check on all the others
samples.evidence:
`sharesAddressWithServer` (image-fetcher.ts:256) returns true if `addresses.some(a => seen.has(a))`, and `assertFetchableImageUrl` acts on that with an unconditional `return` at line 311 — before `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` at line 316 ever runs.

Attack: the document author (image `src` is attacker-influenced, per the file's own docstring) publishes `http://evil.example/x.png` on a host whose port equals the configured server's port. Because `mayBeServer` (line 299-300) compares only the port, any http/https URL on the server's port qualifies. The attacker's nameserver answers with two A records: the public IP of the configured API server (trivially discoverable) plus an internal target (`169.254.169.254`, `10.0.0.5`, `127.0.0.1`). `sharesAddressWithServer` sees the server IP in the set, returns true, and the gate returns ALLOW without ever running `isPrivateAddress` over the internal record. `fetchOrThrow` then resolves independently at connect time and may connect to the internal address (the attacker controls record ordering / TTLs). This is most exploitable when `--server` is plain http (self-hosted / dev), where no TLS name check gets in the way.

The exemption should require that *every* resolved address belongs to the server (or, at minimum, still run `isPrivateAddress` over all addresses before returning).

samples.summary: SSRF gate is TOCTOU-bypassable by DNS rebinding, and the code comment's justification for leaving it open ("undici does not expose" a pinned connection) appears to be incorrect
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the hostname with `lookup` (line 308) and then `fetchOrThrow` (line 363) issues the request by hostname, causing a second, independent resolution. An attacker-controlled nameserver with a ~0s TTL answers the gate's lookup with a public address and the connect-time lookup with `169.254.169.254` / `127.0.0.1`, defeating the whole control. The docstring at lines 266-269 (and `docs/design/cli.md`) accepts this as unavoidable because "closing that needs a pinned connection, which undici does not expose" — undici does expose it: `new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })` passed as `init.dispatcher` lets the caller supply the resolver used for the actual connection, so the gate's verdict can be pinned to the address that is dialed. Accepting a documented residual risk on a false premise is worth flagging: the standard SSRF bypass is left open and the comment discourages anyone from closing it.

samples.summary: `isPrivateAddress` does not cover IPv6 multicast (`ff00::/8`), deprecated site-local (`fec0::/10`), or the IPv4-translated form `::ffff:0:a.b.c.d`
samples.evidence: Tracing `isPrivateAddress` (lines 145-189): after the `::`/`::1`/IPv4-mapped branch it checks only `fc00::/7` (line 159), `fe80::/10` (line 160), NAT64, 6to4 and Teredo. `ff02::1` (all-nodes) and `fec0::/10` fall through to `return false` and are allowed. Likewise `::ffff:0:7f00:1` (RFC 2765 IPv4-translated, `::ffff:0:0/96`) has `words[4] === 0xffff`, so `words.slice(0,5).every(w => w===0)` at line 151 is false and the embedded 127.0.0.1 is never extracted — the address is allowed. On the IPv4 side `192.88.99.0/24` (6to4 relay anycast) is also absent. Each is a narrow gap (TCP to multicast is largely useless, `fec0::/10` is deprecated), but a resolver or a doc `src` returning one of these spellings walks past the gate. I checked the full range table in `isPrivateIPv4`/`isPrivateAddress` and the test table in `packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts`; none of these spellings appear.

samples.summary: The login nonce — the sole secret binding the loopback callback — is printed to stderr and passed as an argv to `open`, exposing it to other local users and to browser history
samples.evidence: Line 179 generates the nonce, line 183 embeds it in `oauthUrl`, line 184 prints the full URL to stderr, and line 189 passes it to `open` (a child process whose command line is readable via `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` by other users on a shared host, and which lands in the browser's address bar/history/extension APIs). The nonce is precisely what stops "another local process or a web page" (login.ts:174-178) from injecting its own code into `startCallbackServer`; any local observer who reads it can complete a callback at line 307 and fix the CLI onto an attacker-chosen account. The lessons doc acknowledges the argv exposure, but the stderr print (captured by CI logs, terminal scrollback, and multiplexer buffers) is an additional channel and is not called out.

samples.summary: Backend continues to mint CLI codes for `?mode=cli` requests carrying no nonce, so the loopback code-injection attack remains fully open for any already-installed CLI
samples.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` (lines 54-57) logs a warning and proceeds when `req.query.nonce` is `undefined`, and `auth.controller.ts:130-134` then omits `&nonce=` from the loopback redirect. Any attacker can therefore still drive `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim's guessed port>` (no nonce), authenticate as themselves, and have the server redirect a valid code to the victim's `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. A current CLI rejects it at login.ts:307, but every published CLI predating this change accepts it and logs the victim into the attacker's account. This is a deliberate, documented compatibility window (guard docstring lines 18-30, docs/design/cli.md), so it is not an oversight — but it is a live exposure window for existing installs, and nothing here (no version floor on `state`, no telemetry gate, no dated removal) bounds it.

samples.summary: `data:` image URLs return from the gate immediately and are then fetched with no size bound
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` line 283 short-circuits for `data:` before any other check, and `createImageFetcher` (line 363) then hands the whole URL to `fetch`, buffering it into a Blob at line 389. A shared document can embed an arbitrarily large `data:` inline (or many of them) and drive the exporting CLI into unbounded memory growth. No `Content-Length`/byte cap exists anywhere in the fetch loop for http(s) responses either.

samples.summary: `redactUrl` strips userinfo, query and fragment but keeps the path, which can itself carry a credential
samples.evidence: redactUrl (lines 94-112) keeps `u.pathname`. Signed image/CDN URLs commonly place the token in a path segment (e.g. `/s/<signature>/img.png`), and the docstring at lines 87-92 justifies the function specifically by "image `src` values routinely carry presigned tokens". Those tokens survive into stderr via `httpError(..., "Image fetch failed: ... for ${redactUrl(target)}")` at image-fetcher.ts:386. Keeping the path is a deliberate diagnosability trade-off, but it leaves a real leak channel for path-signed URLs.

finding.summary: SSRF gate: the "same listener as the configured server" exemption allows a URL when ANY ONE of its resolved addresses matches the server, skipping the private-address check on all the others
finding.evidence:
`sharesAddressWithServer` (image-fetcher.ts:256) returns true if `addresses.some(a => seen.has(a))`, and `assertFetchableImageUrl` acts on that with an unconditional `return` at line 311 — before `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` at line 316 ever runs.

Because `mayBeServer` (line 299-300) compares only the port, any http/https URL on the server's port qualifies. The attacker's nameserver answers with two A records: the public IP of the configured API server (trivially discoverable) plus an internal target (`169.254.169.254`, `10.0.0.5`, `127.0.0.1`). `sharesAddressWithServer` sees the server IP in the set, returns true, and the gate returns ALLOW without ever running `isPrivateAddress` over the internal record. `fetchOrThrow` then resolves independently at connect time and may connect to the internal address (the attacker controls record ordering / TTLs). verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. `sharesAddressWithServer` (image-fetcher.ts:243-257) returns true when ANY single resolved address matches a server address (`addresses.some((a) => seen.has(a.toLowerCase()))`, :256), and `assertFetchableImageUrl` acts on it with an unconditional `return` at :311, short-circuiting both the internal-name throw at :314 and `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` at :316. The exemption's precondition `mayBeServer` (:299-300) compares only `effectivePort`, never the host, so any attacker-chosen hostname on the server's port reaches it (the legitimate server already returned via the exact-origin fast path at :291). `resolveHost` (:204-229) plus `defaultLookup` (:325-326, `{all: true}`) return the full multi-record answer, so an attacker-controlled nameserver returning [server's public IP, 169.254.169.254] causes the gate to ALLOW without ever evaluating the private address. `fetchOrThrow` (:363) resolves independently at connect time — a gap the file itself acknowledges at :266-269 — so the connection can land on the internal address. The vector is reachable: `createImageFetcher` (:357-362) gates document-supplied image `src` values, which the file's own docstring (:55-60) states are attacker-influenced, and every redirect hop re-enters the same weakened path. No guard elsewhere constrains the address set; scheme allow-list (:284) and internal-name check (:306) do not help, and :306 is explicitly bypassed when `mayBeServer` is true. Full exploitation is easiest with a plain-http `--server` (no TLS name check) and depends on connect-time record selection, which lowers exploitability but not the reality of the skipped check. This is SSRF/unsafe input handling, squarely in the Security lane, and is a clear security weakness (major) with no applicable refutation ground.

finding.summary: SSRF gate is TOCTOU-bypassable by DNS rebinding, and the code comment's justification for leaving it open ("undici does not expose" a pinned connection) appears to be incorrect
finding.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the hostname with `lookup` (line 308) and then `fetchOrThrow` (line 363) issues the request by hostname, causing a second, independent resolution. An attacker-controlled nameserver with a ~0s TTL answers the gate's lookup with a public address and the connect-time lookup with `169.254.169.254` / `127.0.0.1`, defeating the whole control. The docstring at lines 266-269 (and `docs/design/cli.md`) accepts this as unavoidable because "closing that needs a pinned connection, which undici does not expose" — undici does expose it: `new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })` passed as `init.dispatcher` lets the caller supply the resolver used for the actual connection, so the gate's verdict can be pinned to the address that is dialed. Accepting a documented residual risk on a false premise is worth flagging: the standard SSRF bypass is left open and the comment discourages anyone from closing it.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. `assertFetchableImageUrl` renders its allow/deny verdict from `resolveHost` → `lookup(url.hostname)` (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:308, :214, :325-326), but the request is then issued by hostname string via `fetchOrThrow(target, { redirect: 'manual' }, fetchImpl)` (image-fetcher.ts:363-367), which forwards straight to `impl(url, init)` (packages/cli/src/errors.ts:162) with no `dispatcher`, no pinned address and no Host rewrite anywhere in the module. That is a genuine TOCTOU: Node/undici performs a second independent resolution at connect time, so an attacker-controlled nameserver with ~0s TTL can answer the gate with a public address and the connect with 169.254.169.254 / 127.0.0.1, defeating the private-address rules at lines 316-322. Redirect hops (lines 361-381) re-enter the same gate and inherit the same window. The justification text is present as quoted at lines 266-269 and mirrored at docs/design/cli.md:886-888; the claim that a pinned connection is unavailable is at minimum contestable, since undici's Agent supports `connect: { lookup }` and Node's fetch accepts `init.dispatcher`, which is precisely the seam that would bind the verdict to the dialed address. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described (not `not-present`); the only rebinding-immune path is the `ipLiteral` short-circuit at lines 82-87/209-210, which does not cover the name case the attack uses, and no other guard, agent config or address pinning exists (not `already-guarded`); and SSRF is explicitly inside this lens's lane, with real impact — attacker-influenced document `src` fetched with the CLI operator's network position and the response bytes embedded into the exported PDF/DOCX the victim opens (not `out-of-scope`).

finding.summary: SSRF gate fails open when the DNS pre-resolution errors (or returns nothing)
finding.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the hostname and, on any rejection from `lookup`, `return`s — i.e. allows the fetch (image-fetcher.ts:203-209). The same happens if the resolver answers with an empty array, since `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` is then false (line 210). The gate's own comment frames this as "let the fetch report it", but the gate and the fetch perform two independent resolutions. An attacker who controls the authoritative nameserver for a `src` host (document content is attacker-influenced — anyone who can edit or share the doc picks the `src`) can answer the gate's `getaddrinfo` with SERVFAIL/timeout and then answer undici's connect-time resolution with `169.254.169.254` or `127.0.0.1`, and the CLI will GET it and embed the bytes in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim opens. Any transient resolver hiccup also silently disables the control for that request. Fail-closed (block, classified as a network error) would preserve the diagnosability the comment is after without turning a resolver error into an allow.

verdict.reason: The claimed fail-open is not present in this repository. The gate's DNS pre-resolution lives in `resolveHost` (image-fetcher.ts:204-229) and fails CLOSED on both conditions the finding names: a `lookup` rejection is caught and re-thrown as `new SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR', 'Could not resolve the host of image URL …')` (lines 215-221), and an empty answer array throws the same SystemError (lines 222-227). There is no `return` that allows the fetch on resolver failure. The cited lines 203-209 are the doc comment plus the IP-literal fast path (`if (literal) return [literal]`, line 210), whose returned literal is still run through `isPrivateAddress` at line 316. `assertFetchableImageUrl` awaits `resolveHost` at line 308 without a catch, so the rejection propagates past `fetchOrThrow` (line 363) and no request is made. The comment at lines 197-203 explicitly documents the fail-closed rationale the finding recommends adopting. The only other `resolveHost` caller, `sharesAddressWithServer` (243-257), catches and returns `false`, which denies the server exemption and narrows rather than widens access. Tests at packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:271-279 and 334-343 assert refusal with no fetch for a loopback-resolving name and for an empty lookup result. Glob confirms a single copy of the file.

finding.summary: isPrivateAddress omits IPv6 transition ranges that embed IPv4 (NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo 2001::/32)
finding.evidence: `isPrivateAddress` handles dotted-quad IPv4, `::`/`::1`, IPv4-mapped/-compatible (`::ffff:*`), `fc00::/7` and `fe80::/10` (lines 131-148), but not the transition prefixes that carry an IPv4 address in later words. On a network with a NAT64 gateway (common on IPv6-only hosts and some CI runners), a `src` of `http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/latest/meta-data/` is a literal, passes `ipLiteral`, is not matched by any rule (words[0]=0x0064 → first=0x00, not fc/fd, not fe80), is allowed, and reaches 169.254.169.254. `2002:7f00:1::` (6to4 → 127.0.0.1) is the same shape. Also unmatched on the IPv4 side: 198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255. Severity reflects the SSRF impact if the deployment has such a gateway; confidence is low because it depends on the host's network having NAT64/6to4 configured.

verdict.reason: The finding asserts `isPrivateAddress` omits NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96), 6to4 (2002::/16) and Teredo (2001::/32), plus IPv4 198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255. All of these are explicitly implemented in the working tree. image-fetcher.ts:167-175 handles the NAT64 well-known prefix (reaching through to the embedded IPv4 and blocking the local-use 64:ff9b:1::/48 sibling), :176-179 handles 6to4 via isPrivateEmbeddedIPv4(words[1], words[2]), and :180-187 handles Teredo including the complemented client IPv4. The reviewer's exact PoC `[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]` parses to words [0x0064,0xff9b,0,0,0,0,0xa9fe,0xa9fe], matches line 167, and yields a=169,b=254 -> true at line 91, so it is blocked; `2002:7f00:1::` matches line 176 -> a=127 -> true at line 90. The IPv4 ranges claimed missing are at lines 95 (192.0.0.0/24), 96 (198.18.0.0/15) and 97 (a >= 224 covering multicast/reserved and 255.255.255.255). Tests pin these exact vectors at packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:187-195 (private) and :205-207 (public embeddings still allowed). The cited line range 131-148 also does not correspond to the described code. Code is not present as described.
